fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and honestly my answer has changed over the past few years. When I started out, the default assumption was that data mixing is basically a hyperparameter search. You have some web text, some code, some math, maybe some multilingual data, and you just try a few proportions and pick whatever gives you the best downstream numbers. And people still do that, and it works to a degree.

But the thing I've come to believe is that the question "what's the right mixture" is kind of ill-posed on its own, because the answer depends enormously on what you measure and when you measure it. If you tune the mix to minimize validation loss on a held-out web split, you'll end up upweighting web data, because of course you will. If you tune it for benchmark performance, you'll upweight whatever looks like the benchmarks. So the first thing I try to do is be very honest about the target. What do I actually want this model to be good at, and does my evaluation reflect that, or is it just a proxy that's easy to compute?

The second thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that the optimal mixture is not stationary across training. Early in training, the model is learning very basic things, like syntax, common facts, and the structure of language. Almost any reasonably diverse data is fine for that. Later on, the model has saturated the easy stuff and the marginal value of a domain changes a lot. Code and math data, for example, seem to give you much more per token late in training than early on, and that's part of why the whole midtraining idea has become so popular. You don't need one mixture. You need a schedule. And a lot of what people are calling "annealing" or "midtraining" is really just the realization that the last ten or twenty percent of training is where you should be most deliberate about what the model sees.

The third thing, and this comes a lot from my earlier work on architectures and on scaling, is that small-scale experiments can mislead you in a specific way. When you do mixture ablations at a small scale, the model doesn't have the capacity to benefit from the harder domains, so those domains look useless, and you downweight them. Then at full scale you discover you've starved the model of exactly the data it could have used. So I try to be careful to either run the ablations at a scale where the model can actually absorb the hard data, or to look at trends across scales rather than a single point.

And then the practical thing is that I think domain balancing and data quality are really the same problem viewed from two angles. If a domain is small but very high quality, you can repeat it a few times and it behaves more like a bigger domain. If a domain is huge but noisy, filtering it is effectively changing the mixture. So rather than thinking "how many percent code," I increasingly think about it as, for each slice of data, how many effective high-quality tokens do I have, and how much of the model's budget is that worth. That reframing tends to give you much more sensible answers than treating the raw proportions as the thing to optimize.

So if I had to summarize: decide what you're actually optimizing for, treat the mixture as a schedule rather than a constant, don't trust tiny-scale ablations on hard domains, and think in terms of effective quality-weighted tokens rather than raw percentages. That's roughly how I approach it right now, but I'll say this is one of the areas where I expect my views to keep moving.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's still more of an art than a science, and I'd be cautious about anyone who claims to have a clean formula for it.

The way I think about it starts with what you actually want the model to be good at. If you care about a broad general-purpose model, you want coverage: web text, code, math, books, scientific papers, multilingual data, and so on. But the right proportions are not obvious from first principles. Domains interact with each other. Code seems to help reasoning more broadly, for example, and some kinds of data look redundant but end up mattering for robustness. So you can't just treat each domain as an independent knob.

In practice, a lot of it is empirical. You run smaller-scale experiments with different mixtures, look at a range of downstream evaluations, and try to find a mixture that doesn't sacrifice too much on any axis. There are more principled approaches now, like learning the mixture weights with a proxy model, or fitting scaling-law-style predictions for how loss on each domain responds to its proportion. Those are useful, but the open question is always whether what you find at small scale transfers to the large model. Sometimes it does and sometimes it doesn't.

One thing I've become more aware of through our work on dataset bias is that "domain" is often a fuzzier concept than we think. When we looked at large-scale image datasets that are supposedly diverse and general, a neural network could still tell with surprisingly high accuracy which dataset an image came from. Each source has its own fingerprint, from how it was collected, filtered, and curated. I think the same is true for text. Two corpora that are both labeled "web data" can be quite different underneath. So balancing domains isn't only about the labels you put on the sources. It's also about understanding what distribution each source really represents.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that quality and diversity often matter more than exact ratios. A smaller amount of really high-quality data in a domain can be worth much more than a lot of noisy data. You also need to watch for over-repetition: if you upsample a small, high-quality domain too aggressively, you start seeing diminishing or even negative returns.

And timing matters. Increasingly people think about the mixture as something that changes over training. You do broad pretraining first, then shift toward higher-quality or more targeted data later, in mid-training or annealing phases. That's become a pretty important lever, because the model seems especially sensitive to what it sees near the end of training.

So my short answer is: start from your goals, make sure you have broad coverage, run careful ablations at a scale you can afford, measure on many different evaluations rather than just one, and stay humble about how well the small-scale results will transfer.

fable-5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of those areas where I think the field still operates more on intuition than on principled methods. When people talk about training large models, the architecture gets a lot of attention, but the data mixture — how much web text versus code versus math versus academic papers — often matters just as much, and it's decided in a surprisingly ad hoc way.

The way I think about it, there are a few levels to the problem. The first is just measuring what you have. Domains aren't cleanly labeled in practice — a web crawl contains code, contains math, contains everything — so before you can balance anything, you need some way to characterize the distribution, whether that's through clustering, classifiers, or metadata.

The second level is deciding what you're optimizing for. If you upweight code, you typically get better reasoning and coding ability, but you might pay for it elsewhere. So the balance really depends on what capabilities you care about downstream. There's no universally correct mixture — it's always relative to your evaluation suite, and that's something people should be honest about.

And then the third level is methodology. The naive approach is to run full training ablations with different mixtures, but that's incredibly expensive at scale. So what we and others have found more practical is to use small proxy models — train many small models with different domain weights, see how performance transfers, and use that to extrapolate or fit some kind of scaling relationship for the mixture itself. The encouraging finding is that mixture rankings are often fairly consistent across scales, so the small-scale signal is genuinely informative, though you have to be careful because some effects, like the benefit of rare high-quality data, only show up once the model is large enough to exploit it.

One more thing I'd add is that it's not just about static proportions. The ordering matters too — this is why people have moved toward multi-stage training, where you might end with a higher concentration of high-quality, curated data in a midtraining or annealing phase. So in some sense "balancing domains" is becoming a question of scheduling over the whole curriculum, not just picking one set of weights at the start. I find that a much richer and more interesting problem.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the least scientific parts of the whole pipeline, and I say that as someone who's spent real time on it.

The first thing I'd push back on is the word "balancing," because it implies the domains are separate buckets and you're allocating a budget across them. Empirically they're not independent at all. Code data makes models better at things that look nothing like code. Math changes how the model handles ordinary reasoning in natural language. So you can't tune the proportions one at a time and add up the results — the interactions are often bigger than the main effects.

The second thing is that there's no mixture that's good in the abstract. You have to name the capabilities you care about, and then the mixture is just whatever maximizes those. In my experience, most arguments about data ratios are actually disguised arguments about objectives — two people want different models and are fighting about percentages. And whatever you can measure well is what you'll end up optimizing, which is its own danger.

And the optimal mixture isn't even a constant over a run. It shifts with scale, and it shifts across training. Early you want breadth; late in training you can upweight narrow high-quality data much more aggressively and it actually sticks, in a way it wouldn't have if you'd front-loaded it.

What makes this hard rather than merely tedious is that small-scale ablations don't transfer reliably. You rank five mixtures with a small proxy model, and the ranking can reorder at the scale you actually care about. So people fall back on priors and a few very expensive runs. I'd like this to become a science. Right now it's closer to cooking.

Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think there's a clean principled answer yet. A lot of it is still empirical.

The way I think about it is to start from what you want the model to be good at, and then work backwards. Web text gives you broad coverage. Code, math, and other specialized domains give you particular skills, and sometimes those skills transfer in ways you wouldn't expect. Code data seems to help with reasoning more generally, for example. So I don't treat each domain as an independent bucket. They interact.

In practice, the most reliable thing is to run small-scale experiments. You train smaller models on different mixtures and see how the downstream evaluations move. It's not perfect, because what works at a small scale doesn't always carry over to a large one, but it gives you a signal that's much better than intuition alone. You also have to be careful about repetition. Upweighting a small, high-quality domain too much just means you're repeating it many times, and the returns drop off quickly.

The other thing I find interesting is that the mixture doesn't have to be fixed over training. You can train mostly on broad data first, then shift toward a more targeted mixture later. That's where midtraining comes in. You get to shape specific capabilities without giving up the general foundation.

And I'd be cautious about the evaluations. If you tune the mixture to a benchmark, you may just be fitting to that benchmark, so I try to keep a diverse set of evaluations in mind.

haiku-5.5.text:
I don't think there's a clean recipe for this, so I start from the goal. The mixture is really a statement about what you want the model to be good at, which means deciding what matters before looking at how much data you happen to have in each domain.

The first thing I want to know is whether the domains actually compete. Sometimes adding more of one helps the others because they share structure, like general reasoning or language patterns. Other times they trade off and you're fighting for capacity. I don't think you can tell which situation you're in by reasoning from first principles. You have to run small, controlled experiments.

I also try not to let the raw size of each source set the balance. A huge domain can drown out a smaller one that's more informative per token. So I think about how much each domain contributes to the capabilities I care about, and then reweight from there. Upsampling a small, high-quality domain later in training is one lever worth considering, though the right schedule depends a lot on scale.

The caveat is that a balance that works at one model size or data budget doesn't always carry over to another. I'd check the mixture at the scale you'll actually deploy at, rather than trusting a ratio that worked somewhere else.

I think the first thing is to ask what you want the model to be good at. Balancing domains doesn’t necessarily mean giving every domain the same amount of data, or sampling everything in proportion to how much you can collect. Some domains have much more data, but that doesn’t automatically make them more useful.

I would start with a reasonably broad mixture and then treat the proportions as something to experiment with. If you increase one domain, what improves, and what gets worse? You need evaluations across domains to see those tradeoffs, because a single average score can hide them.

And the quality of the data matters alongside the quantity. So I don’t think there’s a universal ratio. The right balance depends on the model, the training budget, and the capabilities you care about.
